extracted.intended_audience: DEA registrants, regulated practitioners, administrative/regulatory attorneys, and DEA adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative decision setting out legal standards for revoking or denying DEA practitioner registrations under the Controlled Substances Act, focusing on dispensing from unregistered locations, recordkeeping and dispensing-log requirements, burden of proof, and the five public-interest factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate registration for each principal place of business (21 CFR 1301.12(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] separate registration is required for each principal place of business or professional practice at one general physical location where controlled substances are . . . dispensed by a person." (21 CFR 1301.12(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when a practitioner dispenses or administers controlled substances at a brick-and-mortar location; the so-called 'black bag' exception (traveling to patients' homes) does not apply to a practitioner who maintains a practice location to which patients come. A registrant who dispenses at a second physical clinic must obtain a separate registration for that address; reliance on guidance about travel-to-patient scenarios is not a defense for dispensing at an unregistered clinic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'dispense' includes prescribing and administering (21 U.S.C. 802(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dispense" means "to deliver a controlled substance to an ultimate user . . . including the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance." (21 U.S.C. 802(10))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's act of administering a controlled substance at a location constitutes 'dispensing' for purposes of the registration requirement. Misunderstanding or using a non-statutory meaning of 'dispense' (e.g., equating it only with shipping) is not persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain complete and accurate record of each controlled substance received (21 U.S.C. 827(a)(3); 21 CFR 1304.21(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every registrant who dispenses controlled substances "shall maintain, on a current basis, a complete and accurate record of each such substance . . . received . . . or otherwise disposed of by him . . ." (21 U.S.C. 827(a)(3); 21 CFR 1304.21(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records must be current and readily retrievable from ordinary business records. Failure to have purchase/invoice records or to make them readily retrievable at inspection supports an inference of noncompliance. The statute does not require a perpetual inventory, but completeness and retrievability are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispensing-log data elements required (21 CFR 1304.22(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispenser must maintain records of, among other things, the number of units or volume dispensed, the name and address of the person to whom it was dispensed, the date of dispensing, the number of units or volume dispensed, and the written or typewritten name or initials of the individual who dispensed or administered the substance. (21 CFR 1304.22(c))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements also include drug strength and form and patient address (and other manufacturer-level data where applicable). Logs missing strength, form, recipient address, or other required fields do not comply. Adding some fields after inspection (e.g., addresses) may be insufficient if other required data (e.g., drug strength) remain absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records must be readily retrievable from ordinary business records
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled-substance records must be maintained "readily retrievable from [a registrant's] ordinary business records" and available for inspection (statutory and regulatory recordkeeping framework as applied in 21 U.S.C. 827 and 21 CFR 1304 provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If requested records are not produced at inspection and are within the party's control, courts/agency infer the missing evidence is unfavorable (citing UAW v. NLRB and related authority). Changing computer systems or inability to retrieve records at inspection is not a defense to noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government burden of proof in registration and revocation proceedings (21 CFR 1301.44(d),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under DEA regulations the Government has the burden of proof to grant or deny an application and to revoke or suspend a registration. (21 CFR 1301.44(d) & (e))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Government must present a prima facie case. Once the Government meets its prima facie showing, the burden shifts to the registrant/respondent to show why they can be entrusted with a registration (i.e., to rebut and demonstrate trustworthiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five public-interest factors for registration determinations (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1) A–E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress directed the Attorney General to consider five factors when determining whether registration issuance is inconsistent with the public interest: (A) recommendation of appropriate State licensing board; (B) registrant's experience in dispensing/ research with controlled substances; (C) conviction record relating to controlled substances; (D) compliance with applicable State, Federal, or local laws; (E) such other conduct which may threaten public health and safety. (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors are considered disjunctively and weighed case-by-case; any single factor or combination may be decisive. The agency may rely on any one or a combination of factors and need not make explicit findings on every factor; seriousness of misconduct is central to the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness / acceptance of responsibility as a prerequisite for re-entrustment
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant who has committed acts inconsistent with the public interest must unequivocally accept responsibility for those acts and demonstrate that they will not engage in future misconduct; past performance is the best predictor of future performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency decisions consider whether the respondent unequivocally accepts responsibility and shows concrete remedial measures. Minimizing misconduct, shifting blame, or lack of understanding of statutory responsibilities undermines a showing of trustworthiness. Egregiousness and extent of misconduct, and deterrence needs, influence the sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of deterrence and egregiousness in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency considers specific and general deterrence and the egregiousness and extent of misconduct when determining an appropriate sanction (revocation, denial, suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where misconduct is foundational to the CSA's regulatory scheme (e.g., prolonged dispensing from an unregistered location), a sanction less than revocation may fail to deter both the respondent and the registrant community; case law supports weighting deterrence and egregiousness heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization required for practitioner registration (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attorney General shall register practitioners to dispense controlled substances 'if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State authorization to dispense controlled substances is a statutory prerequisite to federal registration; lack of state authorization is a basis to deny federal registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may credit investigators' testimony and rely on uncontroverted documentary admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjudicating factual disputes, the Agency may credit the testimony of DEA investigators and rely on stipulations, documentary evidence, or the respondent's own admissions where supported by the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility determinations may favor investigators over respondents when documentary evidence and admissions support investigators' account. Multiple testimonial and documentary admissions by a respondent undermine contrary testimony and support factual findings against the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate suspension authority where continued registration presents imminent danger (21 U.S.C. 824(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: An Order to Show Cause and Immediate Suspension of Registration may be issued where continued registration constitutes 'an imminent danger to the public health or safety.' (21 U.S.C. 824(d))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute allows immediate suspension pending adjudication when there is an imminent danger; such procedural tools are part of enforcement where serious diversion or public-safety risk is alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-controlled items storage with controlled substances requires prior written permission (21 CFR 1301.72(b)(8)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-controlled drugs, substances, and other materials may be stored with Schedule III through V controlled substances in secure storage areas provided prior written permission is obtained from the Special Agent in Charge of DEA for the area. (21 CFR 1301.72(b)(8)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations under this provision require proof of lack of written permission; absence of substantial evidence means the agency will not sustain the allegation. This is a limited exception and not a substitute for required security practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records must include manufacturer-level information where required (per 21 CFR 1304.22(c) cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dispenser is also required to 'maintain records with the same information required of manufacturers' pursuant to paragraph (a)(2)(i), (ii), (iv), (vii), and (ix) of the section. (citation in 21 CFR 1304.22(c))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where regulation cross-references manufacturer record requirements, registrants must ensure dispensing records capture the additional manufacturer-level fields; omission of such data can render logs noncompliant.
